claim: Sir2 is an NAD+-dependent protein deacetylase.
source: Silent information regulator 2 (Sir2), an NAD+-dependent protein deacetylase, has been proposed to be a longevity factor that plays important roles in dietary restriction (DR)-mediated lifespan extension.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established characteristic of Sir2.

claim: Sir2 has been proposed to be a longevity factor that plays important roles in dietary restriction (DR)-mediated lifespan extension.
source: Silent information regulator 2 (Sir2), an NAD+-dependent protein deacetylase, has been proposed to be a longevity factor that plays important roles in dietary restriction (DR)-mediated lifespan extension.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references prior research proposing this role.

claim: Sir2's role for DR-mediated lifespan extension depends on cAMP-PKA and casein kinase 2 (CK2) signaling in yeast.
source: In this study, we show that the Sir2's role for DR-mediated lifespan extension depends on cAMP-PKA and casein kinase 2 (CK2) signaling in yeast.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Sir2 partially represses the transcription of PMA1 (encoding an H+-ATPase).
source: Sir2 partially represses the transcription of lifespan-associated genes, such as PMA1 (encoding an H+-ATPase) and many ribosomal protein genes, through deacetylation of Lys 16 of histone H4 in the promoter regions of these genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by qRT-PCR and ChIP data in Figure 1.

claim: Sir2 partially represses the transcription of many ribosomal protein genes.
source: Sir2 partially represses the transcription of lifespan-associated genes, such as PMA1 (encoding an H+-ATPase) and many ribosomal protein genes, through deacetylation of Lys 16 of histone H4 in the promoter regions of these genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2.

claim: Sir2 represses transcription through deacetylation of Lys 16 of histone H4 in the promoter regions of PMA1 and ribosomal protein genes.
source: Sir2 partially represses the transcription of lifespan-associated genes, such as PMA1 (encoding an H+-ATPase) and many ribosomal protein genes, through deacetylation of Lys 16 of histone H4 in the promoter regions of these genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP data showing H4K16 acetylation levels in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Sir2 repression of gene transcription is relieved by Sir2 S473 phosphorylation.
source: This repression is relieved by Sir2 S473 phosphorylation, which is mediated by active cAMP-PKA and CK2 signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing increased PMA1 and RPG expression with Sir2-S473E mutation in Figure 2.

claim: Sir2 S473 phosphorylation is mediated by active cAMP-PKA and CK2 signaling.
source: This repression is relieved by Sir2 S473 phosphorylation, which is mediated by active cAMP-PKA and CK2 signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Phos-tag SDS-PAGE data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Moderate DR increases the replicative lifespan of wild-type yeast.
source: Moderate DR increases the replicative lifespan of wild-type yeast but has no effect on that of yeast expressing the Sir2-S473E or S473A allele, suggesting that the effect of Sir2 on DR-mediated lifespan extension is negatively regulated by S473 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by lifespan data in Figure 4.

claim: Moderate DR has no effect on the replicative lifespan of yeast expressing the Sir2-S473E allele.
source: Moderate DR increases the replicative lifespan of wild-type yeast but has no effect on that of yeast expressing the Sir2-S473E or S473A allele, suggesting that the effect of Sir2 on DR-mediated lifespan extension is negatively regulated by S473 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by lifespan data in Figure 4C.

claim: Moderate DR has no effect on the replicative lifespan of yeast expressing the Sir2-S473A allele.
source: Moderate DR increases the replicative lifespan of wild-type yeast but has no effect on that of yeast expressing the Sir2-S473E or S473A allele, suggesting that the effect of Sir2 on DR-mediated lifespan extension is negatively regulated by S473 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by lifespan data in Figure 4C.

claim: The effect of Sir2 on DR-mediated lifespan extension is negatively regulated by S473 phosphorylation.
source: Moderate DR increases the replicative lifespan of wild-type yeast but has no effect on that of yeast expressing the Sir2-S473E or S473A allele, suggesting that the effect of Sir2 on DR-mediated lifespan extension is negatively regulated by S473 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the lifespan data in Figure 4.

claim: Sirtuins are a highly conserved family of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD)-dependent protein deacetylases.
source: Sirtuins, a highly conserved family of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD)-dependent protein deacetylases, have been implicated as a key metabolic sensor to link dietary restriction (DR) with lifespan extension in yeast, worms, flies, and mice (Longo and Kennedy, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Sirtuins have been implicated as a key metabolic sensor to link dietary restriction (DR) with lifespan extension in yeast, worms, flies, and mice.
source: Sirtuins, a highly conserved family of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD)-dependent protein deacetylases, have been implicated as a key metabolic sensor to link dietary restriction (DR) with lifespan extension in yeast, worms, flies, and mice (Longo and Kennedy, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Longo and Kennedy, 2006.

claim: Sir2 is the founding member of the sirtuin family.
source: In yeast, silent information regulator 2 (Sir2), the founding member of the sirtuin family, mediates transcriptional silencing at the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus, mating type loci and telomeres by deacetylating the acetylated lysine 16 of histone H4 (Rine and Herskowitz, 1987; Hecht et al., 1996; Smith and Boeke, 1997; Imai et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Sir2 mediates transcriptional silencing at the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus, mating type loci and telomeres by deacetylating the acetylated lysine 16 of histone H4.
source: In yeast, silent information regulator 2 (Sir2), the founding member of the sirtuin family, mediates transcriptional silencing at the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus, mating type loci and telomeres by deacetylating the acetylated lysine 16 of histone H4 (Rine and Herskowitz, 1987; Hecht et al., 1996; Smith and Boeke, 1997; Imai et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Sir2 is thought to affect replicative aging of yeast cells by repressing recombination and instability at the rDNA.
source: Sir2 is thought to affect replicative aging of yeast cells by repressing recombination and instability at the rDNA (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997; Falcon and Aris, 2003; Ganley et al., 2009; Stumpferl et al., 2012; Kwan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Sir2 may regulate lifespan by deacetylating H4K16 at sub-telomeric regions.
source: In addition, Sir2 may regulate lifespan by deacetylating H4K16 at sub-telomeric regions (Dang et al., 2009) and by asymmetrically segregating damaged proteins and cellular organelles between mother and daughter cells (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Erjavec and Nystrom, 2007; McFaline-Figueroa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Dang et al., 2009.

claim: Sir2 may regulate lifespan by asymmetrically segregating damaged proteins and cellular organelles between mother and daughter cells.
source: In addition, Sir2 may regulate lifespan by deacetylating H4K16 at sub-telomeric regions (Dang et al., 2009) and by asymmetrically segregating damaged proteins and cellular organelles between mother and daughter cells (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Erjavec and Nystrom, 2007; McFaline-Figueroa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Whether Sir2 mediates lifespan extension by DR in yeast is still under debate.
source: However, whether Sir2 mediates lifespan extension by DR in yeast is still under debate.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citing conflicting studies.

claim: The role of Sir2 in lifespan extension is controversial in worms and flies.
source: Similarly, in worms and flies, the role of Sir2 in lifespan extension is still controversial (Tissenbaum and Guarente, 2001; Rogina and Helfand, 2004; Lee et al., 2006; Wang and Tissenbaum, 2006; Burnett et al., 2011; Viswanathan and Guarente, 2011; Banerjee et al., 2012; Kanfi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations showing conflicting results.

claim: The phosphorylation of Sir2 at S473 is regulated through cAMP-PKA and casein kinase 2 (CK2) signaling.
source: We demonstrate that the phosphorylation of Sir2 at S473, which is regulated through cAMP-PKA and casein kinase 2 (CK2) signaling, determines the role of Sir2 in replicative lifespan (RLS).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The phosphorylation of Sir2 at S473 determines the role of Sir2 in replicative lifespan (RLS).
source: We demonstrate that the phosphorylation of Sir2 at S473, which is regulated through cAMP-PKA and casein kinase 2 (CK2) signaling, determines the role of Sir2 in replicative lifespan (RLS).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by lifespan data in Figure 4.

claim: Deletion of SIR2 is associated with loss of transcriptional silencing at sub-telomeric regions.
source: Deletion of SIR2 is associated with loss of transcriptional silencing at sub-telomeric regions, sterility in haploids, destabilization of rDNA, and shortened lifespan (Kaeberlein et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Kaeberlein et al., 1999.

claim: Deletion of SIR2 is associated with sterility in haploids.
source: Deletion of SIR2 is associated with loss of transcriptional silencing at sub-telomeric regions, sterility in haploids, destabilization of rDNA, and shortened lifespan (Kaeberlein et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Kaeberlein et al., 1999.

claim: Deletion of SIR2 is associated with destabilization of rDNA.
source: Deletion of SIR2 is associated with loss of transcriptional silencing at sub-telomeric regions, sterility in haploids, destabilization of rDNA, and shortened lifespan (Kaeberlein et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Kaeberlein et al., 1999.

claim: Deletion of SIR2 is associated with shortened lifespan.
source: Deletion of SIR2 is associated with loss of transcriptional silencing at sub-telomeric regions, sterility in haploids, destabilization of rDNA, and shortened lifespan (Kaeberlein et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Kaeberlein et al., 1999.

claim: sir2Δ mutant cells are more sensitive than the wild-type strain to high concentrations of NaCl.
source: We observed that sir2Δ mutant cells were more sensitive than the wild-type (WT) strain to high concentrations of NaCl and other monovalent cations, a phenotype not previously associated with loss of Sir2 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 1A.

claim: sir2Δ mutant cells are more sensitive than the wild-type strain to other monovalent cations.
source: We observed that sir2Δ mutant cells were more sensitive than the wild-type (WT) strain to high concentrations of NaCl and other monovalent cations, a phenotype not previously associated with loss of Sir2 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: NaCl sensitivity of sir2Δ mutant is a phenotype not previously associated with loss of Sir2.
source: We observed that sir2Δ mutant cells were more sensitive than the wild-type (WT) strain to high concentrations of NaCl and other monovalent cations, a phenotype not previously associated with loss of Sir2 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a novel observation.

claim: No sensitivity to divalent cations was detected in the sir2Δ mutant.
source: No sensitivity to divalent cations or osmotic stress was detected in the sir2Δ mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No sensitivity to osmotic stress was detected in the sir2Δ mutant.
source: No sensitivity to divalent cations or osmotic stress was detected in the sir2Δ mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The NaCl sensitivity of the sir2Δ mutant was not affected by Fob1.
source: The NaCl sensitivity of the sir2Δ mutant was affected neither by Fob1, which increases the amount of extrachromosomal rDNA circles, nor by pseudodiploid state of the sir2Δ mutant strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fob1 increases the amount of extrachromosomal rDNA circles.
source: The NaCl sensitivity of the sir2Δ mutant was affected neither by Fob1, which increases the amount of extrachromosomal rDNA circles, nor by pseudodiploid state of the sir2Δ mutant strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge about Fob1 function.

claim: The NaCl sensitivity of the sir2Δ mutant was not affected by pseudodiploid state of the sir2Δ mutant strain.
source: The NaCl sensitivity of the sir2Δ mutant was affected neither by Fob1, which increases the amount of extrachromosomal rDNA circles, nor by pseudodiploid state of the sir2Δ mutant strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The plasma membrane potential (ΔΨ) is a critical determinant of cation tolerance.
source: The plasma membrane potential (ΔΨ) is a critical determinant of cation tolerance (Navarre and Goffeau, 2000), and we reasoned that the NaCl sensitivity of the sir2Δ mutant could be due to hyperpolarization of the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Navarre and Goffeau, 2000.

claim: The sir2Δ mutant is more sensitive to the ΔΨ-dependent antibiotic Hygromycin B than the WT strain.
source: Indeed, relative to the WT strain, the sir2Δ mutant was more sensitive to the ΔΨ-dependent antibiotic Hygromycin B (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and had a higher ΔΨ (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The sir2Δ mutant has a higher plasma membrane potential (ΔΨ) than the WT strain.
source: Indeed, relative to the WT strain, the sir2Δ mutant was more sensitive to the ΔΨ-dependent antibiotic Hygromycin B (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and had a higher ΔΨ (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by DiOC6 staining data in Figure 1B.

claim: Reduced potassium uptake is unlikely to contribute to the membrane hyperpolarization in the sir2Δ mutant.
source: Reduced potassium uptake was unlikely to contribute to the membrane hyperpolarization because potassium chloride did not reverse the NaCl-sensitive phenotype of the sir2Δ mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Elevated levels of both PMA1 mRNA and protein levels are observed in sir2Δ cells.
source: In contrast, we observed elevated levels of both PMA1 mRNA and protein levels in sir2Δ cells, which could not be rescued by expression of the enzymatically inactive sir2-H364Y allele (Tanny et al., 1999) (Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR and Western blot data in Figures 1C-E.

claim: Elevated PMA1 expression in sir2Δ cells could not be rescued by expression of the enzymatically inactive sir2-H364Y allele.
source: In contrast, we observed elevated levels of both PMA1 mRNA and protein levels in sir2Δ cells, which could not be rescued by expression of the enzymatically inactive sir2-H364Y allele (Tanny et al., 1999) (Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: Overexpression of Sir2 decreased NaCl sensitivity relative to WT cells.
source: Further, overexpression of Sir2 decreased NaCl sensitivity and Pma1 expression relative to WT cells (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 1G.

claim: Overexpression of Sir2 decreased Pma1 expression relative to WT cells.
source: Further, overexpression of Sir2 decreased NaCl sensitivity and Pma1 expression relative to WT cells (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1H.

claim: Sir2 binding at the PMA1 promoter region is significantly greater than at another DNA fragment 2 kb upstream of the PMA1 promoter.
source: Indeed, Sir2 binding at the PMA1 promoter region was significantly greater than at another DNA fragment 2 kb upstream of the PMA1 promoter, although it was not as great as at other Sir2-regulated sites, specifically Tel-VIR and HMR (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ChIP data in Figure 1I.

claim: Sir2 binding at the PMA1 promoter region is not as great as at other Sir2-regulated sites, specifically Tel-VIR and HMR.
source: Indeed, Sir2 binding at the PMA1 promoter region was significantly greater than at another DNA fragment 2 kb upstream of the PMA1 promoter, although it was not as great as at other Sir2-regulated sites, specifically Tel-VIR and HMR (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ChIP data in Figure 1I.

claim: The H4K16 acetylation level in the PMA1 promoter region is substantially higher in the sir2Δ mutant than in the WT strain.
source: Accordingly, the H4K16 acetylation level in the PMA1 promoter region was substantially higher in the sir2Δ mutant than in the WT strain (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ChIP data in Figure 1J.

claim: Sas2 is a major H4K16 acetyltransferase that antagonizes the effects of Sir2 on telomeric silencing and RLS in yeast.
source: We next tested whether Sas2, a major H4K16 acetyltransferase that antagonizes the effects of Sir2 on telomeric silencing and RLS in yeast (Kimura et al., 2002; Suka et al., 2002; Dang et al., 2009), opposes the Sir2-dependent H4K16 deacetylation in the PMA1 promoter region.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: A sas2Δ mutant shows lower Pma1 mRNA levels than WT cells.
source: A sas2Δ mutant showed lower Pma1 mRNA levels and less H4K16 acetylation in the PMA1 promoter region than WT cells (Heise and et al., 2012), although higher PMA1 expression and H4K16 acetylation in a sir2Δ sas2Δ mutant suggest additional H4K16 acetyltransferases, for example, Esa1 (Clarke et al., 1999; Suka et al., 2001; Chang and Pillus, 2009), replacing for Sas2 in the absence of Sir2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: A sas2Δ mutant shows less H4K16 acetylation in the PMA1 promoter region than WT cells.
source: A sas2Δ mutant showed lower Pma1 mRNA levels and less H4K16 acetylation in the PMA1 promoter region than WT cells (Heise and et al., 2012), although higher PMA1 expression and H4K16 acetylation in a sir2Δ sas2Δ mutant suggest additional H4K16 acetyltransferases, for example, Esa1 (Clarke et al., 1999; Suka et al., 2001; Chang and Pillus, 2009), replacing for Sas2 in the absence of Sir2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ChIP data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Higher PMA1 expression and H4K16 acetylation in a sir2Δ sas2Δ mutant suggest additional H4K16 acetyltransferases, for example, Esa1, replacing for Sas2 in the absence of Sir2.
source: A sas2Δ mutant showed lower Pma1 mRNA levels and less H4K16 acetylation in the PMA1 promoter region than WT cells (Heise and et al., 2012), although higher PMA1 expression and H4K16 acetylation in a sir2Δ sas2Δ mutant suggest additional H4K16 acetyltransferases, for example, Esa1 (Clarke et al., 1999; Suka et al., 2001; Chang and Pillus, 2009), replacing for Sas2 in the absence of Sir2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, with citations to support the role of Esa1.

claim: Sir2 plays an important role in maintaining the ΔΨ in yeast through regulation of PMA1 expression via deacetylation of H4K16 in the PMA1 promoter.
source: Taken together, these data support the model that Sir2 plays an important role in maintaining the ΔΨ in yeast through regulation of PMA1 expression via deacetylation of H4K16 in the PMA1 promoter, while Sas2 antagonizes this function by acetylating H4K16 at this site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Sas2 antagonizes Sir2 function by acetylating H4K16 at the PMA1 promoter.
source: Taken together, these data support the model that Sir2 plays an important role in maintaining the ΔΨ in yeast through regulation of PMA1 expression via deacetylation of H4K16 in the PMA1 promoter, while Sas2 antagonizes this function by acetylating H4K16 at this site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Hyperactivation of the cyclic AMP (cAMP)-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) results in sensitivity to cellular stresses.
source: Prior studies have shown that hyperactivation of the cyclic AMP (cAMP)-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) results in sensitivity to cellular stresses (Stanhill et al., 1999) and NaCl (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and PKA signaling has been proposed to negatively regulate Sir2 in response to glucose availability (Lin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Stanhill et al., 1999.

claim: Hyperactivation of PKA results in sensitivity to NaCl.
source: Prior studies have shown that hyperactivation of the cyclic AMP (cAMP)-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) results in sensitivity to cellular stresses (Stanhill et al., 1999) and NaCl (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and PKA signaling has been proposed to negatively regulate Sir2 in response to glucose availability (Lin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PKA signaling has been proposed to negatively regulate Sir2 in response to glucose availability.
source: Prior studies have shown that hyperactivation of the cyclic AMP (cAMP)-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) results in sensitivity to cellular stresses (Stanhill et al., 1999) and NaCl (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and PKA signaling has been proposed to negatively regulate Sir2 in response to glucose availability (Lin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Lin et al., 2000.

claim: Deletion of PDE2 increases the intracellular cAMP level without affecting Sir2 expression.
source: We deleted PDE2, encoding a high-affinity cAMP phosphodiesterase, which increased the intracellular cAMP level without affecting Sir2 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-H.

claim: The pde2Δ mutant is as sensitive to NaCl as the sir2Δ mutant.
source: The pde2Δ mutant was as sensitive to NaCl as the sir2Δ mutant and increased the Pma1 mRNA level as high as the sir2Δ mutant (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by growth assay data in Figure 2A.

claim: The pde2Δ mutant increases the Pma1 mRNA level as high as the sir2Δ mutant.
source: The pde2Δ mutant was as sensitive to NaCl as the sir2Δ mutant and increased the Pma1 mRNA level as high as the sir2Δ mutant (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2B.

claim: The addition of 8-Bromo-cAMP, a non-hydrolyzable cAMP analog, into the culture medium mimics the effect of the SIR2 deletion on PMA1 expression.
source: Furthermore, the addition of 8-Bromo-cAMP, a non-hydrolyzable cAMP analog, into the culture medium mimicked the effect of the SIR2 deletion on PMA1 expression (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2C.

claim: The Pma1 mRNA level in the pde2Δ tpk1/2/3Δ mutant strain is similar to that in WT.
source: To examine whether PKA is essential for PMA1 regulation, we deleted TPK1, TPK2, and TPK3, the genes encoding the catalytic subunits of PKA, from the pde2Δ mutant strain. The Pma1 mRNA level in the pde2Δ tpk1/2/3Δ mutant strain was similar to that in WT (Figure 2D), therefore, we concluded that cAMP-PKA signaling controls the ability of Sir2 to regulate PMA1 transcription.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2D.

claim: cAMP-PKA signaling controls the ability of Sir2 to regulate PMA1 transcription.
source: To examine whether PKA is essential for PMA1 regulation, we deleted TPK1, TPK2, and TPK3, the genes encoding the catalytic subunits of PKA, from the pde2Δ mutant strain. The Pma1 mRNA level in the pde2Δ tpk1/2/3Δ mutant strain was similar to that in WT (Figure 2D), therefore, we concluded that cAMP-PKA signaling controls the ability of Sir2 to regulate PMA1 transcription.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data in Figure 2D.

claim: The Sir2 binding efficiency at the PMA1 promoter is unaffected in the pde2Δ mutant.
source: To investigate how cAMP-PKA signaling regulates Sir2 activity in the PMA1 promoter, we measured the H4K16 acetylation level and the amount of Sir2 bound to the PMA1 promoter in the pde2Δ mutant. The Sir2 binding efficiency was unaffected, but the H4K16 acetylation level was increased in the pde2Δ mutant (Figure 2E,F), suggesting that active cAMP-PKA signaling inhibits Sir2 activity but not Sir2-binding efficiency.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ChIP data in Figure 2E.

claim: The H4K16 acetylation level at the PMA1 promoter is increased in the pde2Δ mutant.
source: To investigate how cAMP-PKA signaling regulates Sir2 activity in the PMA1 promoter, we measured the H4K16 acetylation level and the amount of Sir2 bound to the PMA1 promoter in the pde2Δ mutant. The Sir2 binding efficiency was unaffected, but the H4K16 acetylation level was increased in the pde2Δ mutant (Figure 2E,F), suggesting that active cAMP-PKA signaling inhibits Sir2 activity but not Sir2-binding efficiency.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ChIP data in Figure 2F.

claim: Active cAMP-PKA signaling inhibits Sir2 activity but not Sir2-binding efficiency.
source: To investigate how cAMP-PKA signaling regulates Sir2 activity in the PMA1 promoter, we measured the H4K16 acetylation level and the amount of Sir2 bound to the PMA1 promoter in the pde2Δ mutant. The Sir2 binding efficiency was unaffected, but the H4K16 acetylation level was increased in the pde2Δ mutant (Figure 2E,F), suggesting that active cAMP-PKA signaling inhibits Sir2 activity but not Sir2-binding efficiency.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: The pde2Δ cells show more Sir2 phosphorylation than the WT and pde2Δ tpk1/2/3Δ cells.
source: To investigate how cAMP-PKA signaling inhibits Sir2 activity, we analyzed the phosphorylation of Sir2 in WT, pde2Δ, and pde2Δ tpk1/2/3Δ cells. The pde2Δ cells showed more Sir2 phosphorylation than the WT and pde2Δ tpk1/2/3Δ cells, suggesting that active cAMP-PKA signaling increases Sir2 phosphorylation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Phos-tag SDS-PAGE data in Figure 2G.

claim: Active cAMP-PKA signaling increases Sir2 phosphorylation.
source: To investigate how cAMP-PKA signaling inhibits Sir2 activity, we analyzed the phosphorylation of Sir2 in WT, pde2Δ, and pde2Δ tpk1/2/3Δ cells. The pde2Δ cells showed more Sir2 phosphorylation than the WT and pde2Δ tpk1/2/3Δ cells, suggesting that active cAMP-PKA signaling increases Sir2 phosphorylation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data in Figure 2G.

claim: Sir2 S473 is a conserved phosphorylation site in all known Sir2 homologs.
source: We examined whether Sir2 S473, a conserved phosphorylation site in all known Sir2 homologs (Gerhart-Hines et al., 2011), is responsible for the regulation of Sir2 deacetylase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Gerhart-Hines et al., 2011.

claim: Mutation of the S473 residue to alanine (Sir2-S473A) abolishes the Sir2 phosphorylation induced by cAMP-PKA signaling.
source: Mutation of the S473 residue to alanine (Sir2-S473A) abolished the Sir2 phosphorylation induced by cAMP-PKA signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Pma1 mRNA level increases in WT cells expressing the phospho-mimetic Sir2-S473E protein.
source: Moreover, the Pma1 mRNA level increased in WT cells expressing the phospho-mimetic Sir2-S473E protein and decreased in pde2Δ cells expressing the phospho-deficient Sir2-S473A protein, matching the respective levels in WT and pde2Δ cells expressing WT Sir2 (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2H.

claim: The Pma1 mRNA level decreases in pde2Δ cells expressing the phospho-deficient Sir2-S473A protein.
source: Moreover, the Pma1 mRNA level increased in WT cells expressing the phospho-mimetic Sir2-S473E protein and decreased in pde2Δ cells expressing the phospho-deficient Sir2-S473A protein, matching the respective levels in WT and pde2Δ cells expressing WT Sir2 (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2H.

claim: The occupancy of H4K16 acetylation in the PMA1 promoter region is higher in the WT cells expressing Sir2-S473E than in cells expressing WT Sir2.
source: Consistently, the occupancy of H4K16 acetylation in the PMA1 promoter region was higher in the WT cells expressing Sir2-S473E and lower in the pde2Δ cells expressing Sir2-S473A than that in the cells expressing WT Sir2 (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ChIP data in Figure 2I.

claim: The occupancy of H4K16 acetylation in the PMA1 promoter region is lower in the pde2Δ cells expressing Sir2-S473A than in cells expressing WT Sir2.
source: Consistently, the occupancy of H4K16 acetylation in the PMA1 promoter region was higher in the WT cells expressing Sir2-S473E and lower in the pde2Δ cells expressing Sir2-S473A than that in the cells expressing WT Sir2 (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ChIP data in Figure 2I.

claim: Sir2 S473 is phosphorylated in response to cAMP-PKA signaling.
